newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco cos challenging Florida's sunshine law.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco cos challenging Florida's sunshine law.

text.p: Tobacco companies fighting a Florida state lawsuit are challenging the constitutionality of the state's sunshine law requiring courtroom disclosure of trade secrets if the proprietary information affects public safety.

William Rutter, a special master appointed by the trial judge in Florida's lawsuit claiming $1 billion from tobacco companies, on Tuesday scheduled a hearing for April 8 on the constitutionality of Florida's Litigation in the Sunshine Act.

Rutter, in turn, would make a recommendation to Palm Beach County Circuit Court Judge, Harold Cohen, who has set an August 4 start for a trial on Florida's suit against cigarette makers. Florida and 21 other states are suing cigarette makers for an estimated $30 billion spent treating sick smokers.

Attorneys in the Florida suit have been skirmishing for months over which industry documents should be presented at trial, including the ones Brooke Group Ltd's Liggett promised to deliver for use against fellow cigarette makers.

Tobacco company attorneys claim broadly that most documents, including some widely available on the Internet and in books, remain privileged communications entitled to be kept from opposing lawyers for use at trial.
Anti-tobacco lawyers claim some of the documents prove tobacco companies conspired to keep from the public scientific evidence of the health dangers of smoking.

Justus Reid, a lawyer for Lorrilard Tobacco Co, a unit of Loews Corp, said the Florida law runs counter to state and federal laws sheltering trade secrets. "It evades the rule-making power of the court, which is contrary to the constitution," Reid said.
An attorney pressing Florida's case said a ruling against the state on the sunshine law would keep the information from news and health organization, as well as jurors in the case.
"If the documents involve a hazardous product, then the public has a right to know their contents," said attorney Michael Maher.

Sandy Bohrer, an attorney representing The New York Times, The Miami Herald and other news organizations, said, "The purpose of the act is to ensure public access to information regarding potential health hazards."
